Live trades on the sampled pools

Everywhere else on this site a trade is a 24-hour aggregate someone else computed. Here it is a transaction. Every swap against a tokenized-stock pool on Solana is a signature on that pool's address, so the trade can be read from the chain itself: which mint moved, in which direction, at what price, paid for by which wallet. That is only true of the DEX pools. The exchanges that list these tokens publish no per-trade feed without a key, so this page covers the sampled pools and nothing else. Nothing below is interpolated or smoothed: the tape shows decoded transactions, and the replay animates only the hours that were collected.

The tape

The accumulating database history, newest first and loaded 20 trades at a time. The page re-reads it every few minutes, so a new collection appears on page one without a reload. The 24-hour replay below uses the collector's complete rolling capture.

The twenty newest decoded swaps, newest first. A buy is the pool losing the tokenized stock to a buyer, a sell is the pool gaining it. The side is read from the pool's own balance change; transaction labels are ignored. Price is USD where the pool's quote token has a USD rate, otherwise the price in the quote token itself. routed marks a transaction that moved more than two mints: an aggregator or arbitrage path in which this pool was one leg.

    How this page is made

    • What the tape covers. The sampled Solana DEX pools only: the top pools by 24-hour volume across the tokenized-stock mints, refreshed on every collector run. There are no CEX trades here at all: the exchanges listing these tokens publish per-trade data only behind a key, so a token that trades mostly on an exchange will look quiet on this page even when it is active.
    • How a trade is decoded. Each swap is read from the transaction's own token balances, before and after, restricted to the accounts the pool owns. The pool's change in the tracked mint is the size; its change in the quote mint is what was paid; the price is one divided by the other, converted to USD with the pool's quote rate. The side follows from the direction: a pool that gained the token was sold into. Nothing is taken from an instruction name or a log line, so a swap routed through an aggregator is decoded exactly like a direct one, and marked routed when the transaction moved more than two mints.
    • Why failed transactions are shown. Most signatures on a busy Solana pool never trade: they are bots racing each other and losing, and they fail. They have to be counted to read the tape correctly: a pool with a 90% failure rate has heavy competition to trade, and much less real trading than its signature count suggests. The failed share is per pool on the chips, and over the whole window in the header line. Failed transactions are counted, never fetched and never decoded, so they cost nothing and can never enter the tape.
    • What the replay shows. It animates the collected trades and only those. An hour that began before collection started is hatched, because it was never sampled: a short bar there means we were not collecting yet. Trades may still have happened. Volume is priced with each pool's own quote rate at collection time, so a stale rate makes a stale USD number. The trade counts never depend on a price.
    • Distinct traders are counted as distinct fee-payer wallets over the hours the cursor has passed, from the trades themselves rather than by summing the per-hour counts, which would count one wallet once per hour it traded in. An aggregator or a relayer can pay the fee for someone else's swap, so read this as distinct paying wallets.
    • How fresh it is. RWA Sonar's server collects once an hour: it reads the newest signatures of each sampled pool from a Solana RPC, fetches a capped number of the successful ones, decodes them and stores them. This page only reads what the server stored (your browser never contacts a Solana node) and re-reads it every five minutes. So the tape is up to about an hour behind the chain, and it samples each pool once an hour. It does not capture every trade: on the busiest pools more swaps happen between collections than one collection reads.
